cards.body: NASA's new plan makes Artemis III a 14-day Earth-orbit test in 2027, where Orion docks with Blue Origin and SpaceX lander prototypes. Artemis IV would then attempt the actual landing in 2028.
cards.more:
Both landers are still in development, so the docking tests are a dress rehearsal before anyone descends to the surface.
NASA says rocket processing times have been cut by about half, and that one in-house fuel-line part cost about a tenth of an outside quote. Those are the agency's own figures.
Axiom Space is also building a lighter 'Sortie' suit, about half the weight of its main suit, for early moonwalks.
cards.title: NASA now aims to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028

cards.body: Caltech's ASTRA payload, launched in March, autonomously extended two pre-built truss sections and built a third in orbit. The team calls it the first self-directed construction of a structure in space.
cards.more:
The full design is a reflector antenna 1.4 metres wide made of 11 bays. The team does not expect to finish all 11 before the mission ends in December.
Controllers only got 7 or 8 contact windows a day, each about 15 minutes, which is why autonomy mattered.
Building in orbit could one day allow structures far larger than anything that fits inside a rocket.
cards.title: A robot assembled part of an antenna in orbit on its own

cards.body: ESA's Prometheus engine completed several hot-fire tests in Germany on 29 October, burning liquid oxygen and methane. It reignited repeatedly without a high-pressure starter, a key trick for reusable rockets.
cards.more:
Its combustion chamber was made by cold gas spray, a form of 3D printing that fuses metal powder at high speed.
ESA describes its power as similar to the Vulcain 2.1 engine on Ariane 6.
An improved 'Mark 2' version is next.
cards.title: Europe's reusable Prometheus engine fired on liquid methane

cards.body: ETH Zurich's ECHO implant uses a gold-and-platinum electrode to turn glucose into gluconate, which mice mostly excreted. It kept blood sugar normal for days without medication in mice with type 2 diabetes.
cards.more:
It switches on when a glucose monitor detects high sugar, and is powered wirelessly by radio.
No ill effects showed up in studies lasting up to six weeks. Outside experts warn that mouse results often fail to carry over to people.
The team plans rabbit and pig studies before any human trials. This is far from clinical use.
cards.title: A tiny implant burned off excess blood sugar in diabetic mice

cards.body: Pantethine, a vitamin B5 derivative, calmed overactive immune cells and prevented psoriasis in mice. In a 24-person trial, patients adding it to standard ointment improved more over 12 weeks.
cards.more:
The target is a family of enzymes called Vanins, which ran unusually high in immune cells from people with psoriasis.
The benefit was clearest in patients with high cholesterol at the start.
The authors call it a proof of concept that needs larger trials. It is not a reason to self-treat.
cards.title: A vitamin B5 supplement eased psoriasis in a small early trial

cards.body: Muscle from people with type 2 diabetes carried more Miro1, a protein that moves mitochondria around. Removing it restored insulin response in lab models, and aerobic exercise lowered it in a trial.
cards.more:
Mitochondria are the cell's power plants, and how they're positioned affects how muscle handles sugar.
The exercise link is an association within one trial, alongside better insulin sensitivity.
Whether drugs could safely target Miro1 in people is still unknown.
cards.title: A muscle protein called Miro1 may help drive type 2 diabetes

cards.body: Among 120,000+ older Hong Kong patients, those on nitrogen-containing bisphosphonates had 16% lower dementia risk than untreated patients and 24% lower than users of other bone drugs. It's an association, not proof.
cards.more:
Common examples are alendronate and zoledronate, used to prevent fractures in osteoporosis.
The link looked stronger in women and in people who'd had a hip fracture.
The authors estimate that treating 48 patients for five years might prevent one case, and call for trials to test cause and effect.
cards.title: Bone-drug users had lower dementia rates in Hong Kong records

cards.body: Marine snow, falling clumps of dead plankton and debris, pulls over 10 gigatons of carbon from surface waters yearly. Lab work suggests the stickiest clumps resist bacteria and deliver up to six times more carbon deep down.
cards.more:
Only about 2 gigatons a year sink deep enough to stay stored for centuries.
Researchers measured stickiness with tiny fluorescent probes under a 3D microscope, a method that took four years to get working.
The six-fold figure comes from experiments and simulations, not open-ocean measurements.
cards.title: Stickier ocean 'snow' carries far more carbon to the deep

cards.body: Sequencing samples taken in 1978 turned up human DNA from several lineages, plus traces of wheat, maize, peanuts, cattle, cats, dogs and Mediterranean red coral. Salt-loving microbes were there too.
cards.more:
Maize and peanuts come from the Americas, a hint that much of the DNA arrived over later centuries of handling and display.
The researchers say the DNA cannot date the cloth or settle its authenticity, because the traces built up at very different times.
cards.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin is a mix of many centuries of contact

cards.body: Archaeologists at Qinngua, near Erik the Red's farm, found a skeleton buried head-to-east, the Christian custom. It confirms the building as a church, the first Norse church found in Greenland in over 60 years.
cards.more:
Its large size and hewn stones suggest AD 1100–1300, though the burial may be older.
Six churches are now known around Erik's settlement of Brattahlíð.
Researchers tentatively link it to a medieval church named in old records, but that is unconfirmed.
cards.title: A grave confirmed a lost Norse church in southern Greenland

cards.body: 3D imaging of the Scottish outlaw's tombstone at Balquhidder shows an early Christian cross, likely carved for a medieval cleric up to 1,000 years before his death in 1734. Later owners added new carvings.
cards.more:
A sword, tongs and a hunting scene were added in the 1400s or 1500s.
A kilted figure with a shield, thought to be MacGregor himself, dates to his own lifetime.
Reusing a fine old stone was common practice, so one slab can hold several eras.
cards.title: Rob Roy's gravestone may be centuries older than Rob Roy

cards.body: Polish-led teams found almost 100 Acheulean hand axes in Botswana's Okwa Valley, about 40 at one ancient lakeshore site with the chips left from making them. Their exact age isn't known yet.
cards.more:
Acheulean tools appeared in Africa about 1.7 million years ago and lasted in places until around 200,000 years ago.
Quarrying for calcrete exposed old river and lake deposits, showing a much wetter Kalahari in the past.
The finds will be compared with tools from further north and from South Africa.
cards.title: Nearly 100 ancient hand axes turned up in the Kalahari

cards.body: MIT and UBC's WorldParticle treats every material as particles and predicts their next positions step by step. One model handled six kinds of physics, and its authors claim proteins ran about 100 times faster.
cards.more:
Normally each material needs its own hand-coded simulator.
The speed figure is the researchers' own comparison with numerical simulators.
The team calls it a first step toward a general 'foundation model' for physical simulation.
cards.title: One AI model simulates sand, soft objects and folding proteins

cards.body: MIT and NYU's FLEX system uses a language model to widen a simple instruction. Told 'don't spill on my laptop', a simulated robot also steered around a nearby phone without being asked.
cards.more:
It works in three steps: add the feature named, generalize it with GPT-4o, then mask out what doesn't matter. The whole process takes about five seconds.
Tests so far were in simulation only, with tasks like serving coffee and carrying a bowling ball.
cards.title: Robots learned to read between the lines of a command

cards.body: China's producer prices rose 5.7% from a year earlier in October, the fastest in over four years, driven by oil and AI-related demand. Consumer prices rose just 0.7%, below forecasts.
cards.more:
Consumer prices were flat from September. Petrol rose 4.2% in the month, but cheaper eggs, vegetables and fruit pulled the index down.
Analysts say weak household demand is keeping shop prices low even as costs climb for factories.
Some expect the energy shock to fade next year.
cards.title: China's factory prices jumped 5.7% while shop prices barely rose

cards.body: Year-on-year price changes. Factories are paying much more for inputs, but little of it has reached shoppers.
cards.title: China's factory inflation is running far ahead of consumer prices

cards.body: MTG-I2 sent its first images, including fog over central Europe and wildfire smoke in Portugal. Full service is expected in 2027.

stat.label: between full scans of Europe and North Africa in rapid-scan mode

cards.title: Europe's new weather satellite can rescan Europe every 2.5 minutes

beats: The closer a satellite orbits, the faster it must go to avoid falling back.
At about 36,000 km up, one orbit takes exactly as long as Earth takes to spin once.
Place it above the equator, moving the same way Earth turns, and it keeps pace with the ground.
From below, it seems frozen in the sky, staring at the same half of the planet.
That's why weather satellites and many TV dishes sit there: the view never moves.
cards.title: Why a weather satellite can hang over one spot

beats: Today, DNA stores genes and proteins do the work, but each needs the other to exist.
RNA can do both jobs: it carries information and, folded right, speeds up chemical reactions.
So scientists proposed early life ran on RNA alone, before DNA and proteins took over.
Labs have since made a 45-letter RNA that can copy other RNA strands.
The open question: would a self-copying molecule count as alive without a metabolism?
cards.title: The RNA world: how life might have started without DNA

beats: The consumer price index, CPI, tracks what households pay for a basket of goods and services.
The producer price index, PPI, tracks what factories get paid for their output.
PPI often moves first, because costs like oil and metals hit factories before shoppers.
If demand is weak, firms may swallow those costs instead of raising shop prices.
So a wide gap between PPI and CPI can mean squeezed profits and cautious consumers.
cards.title: Factory prices versus shop prices: PPI and CPI

beats: A drug 'cuts risk by 20%' sounds big, but it doesn't say how big the risk was.
Absolute risk reduction is the plain drop, say from 10 cases in 100 to 8.
Number needed to treat is one divided by that drop: here, 1 ÷ 0.02 = 50.
It means treating 50 people to prevent one case, a figure anyone can weigh.
Today's dementia study estimated 48 patients over five years per case prevented.
cards.title: 'Number needed to treat' turns risk into people

beats: Anton Chekhov advised writers: if a rifle hangs on the wall in act one, it must fire later.
The point is that every vivid detail makes a quiet promise to the reader.
Break the promise too often and readers feel cheated, or stop paying attention.
Keep it, and a small early detail pays off as a satisfying surprise.
Writers also bend it on purpose, planting false leads called red herrings.
cards.title: Chekhov's gun: don't show what you won't use

beats: Each eye has a spot with no light sensors, where the optic nerve leaves the retina.
That creates a real gap in what each eye detects, a little off-centre.
You never notice because the other eye covers it, and the brain fills in the rest.
It guesses from surrounding colour and pattern, like a photo editor's content-aware fill.
Close one eye and move a dot sideways, and you can make it vanish.
cards.title: Your brain paints over a hole in your vision

myth.claim: Most of your brain sits idle, waiting to be unlocked.
myth.truth: Brain scans show activity across virtually every region over a day, and damage to almost any area causes problems. The brain is about 2% of body weight but burns roughly 20% of its energy, far too costly to leave mostly unused.

cards.title: We only use 10% of our brains

myth.claim: Drop a hammer and a feather, and the hammer wins because it's heavier.
myth.truth: Without air, everything falls at the same rate. Air resistance slows the feather, not its lightness. Apollo 15's David Scott showed it on the Moon in 1971: hammer and feather landed together.

cards.title: Heavier objects fall faster

myth.claim: A desert means scorching sand dunes.
myth.truth: A desert is defined by how little rain or snow falls, not heat. By that measure Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth. Most deserts are rocky or gravelly, with dunes covering only a fraction.

cards.title: Deserts are always hot and sandy

quiz.q: Which Norse explorer founded the first settlements in Greenland, around AD 985?
quiz.why: Erik the Red, exiled from Iceland, led settlers there and named it 'Greenland' to attract them. His son Leif later sailed on to North America.

cards.title: Who led the first Norse settlers to Greenland?

quiz.q: The word 'psoriasis' comes from a Greek word meaning what?
quiz.why: It comes from Greek psora, 'itch'. The ending -iasis marks a condition, as in other medical terms.

cards.title: The itch hiding in the word 'psoriasis'

options: Relative risk fell 50%, absolute risk fell 1 point
Relative risk fell 1%, absolute risk fell 50%
quiz.q: Risk falls from 2 in 100 to 1 in 100. Which statement is true?
quiz.why: Halving is a 50% relative drop, but only 1 person in 100 benefits. That's why headlines quoting only relative risk can sound bigger than they are.

cards.title: A drug drops risk from 2% to 1%. How much did it cut risk?

cards.body: Sandia physicists simulated X-ray blasts on asteroids built from real 3D shapes. One test changed an asteroid's speed by 3.9 mm/s from one direction but only 0.8 mm/s from another. Spin changes varied up to 17-fold.
cards.more:
The model covers vapor blasted off the surface. It does not predict whether the whole body would break apart, which the team says can't yet be done accurately.
The method needs an asteroid's shape from every direction, data that may not exist in time for a real threat.
Delivering and positioning a device would also be extremely hard.
cards.title: Which side you nuke an asteroid from changes how far it moves

cards.body: JAXA's Martian Moons eXploration launched on October 20 and reaches Mars in 2027. Phobos, about 27 km long, has roughly 1/1,800 of Earth's gravity. The mission aims to bring back at least 10 grams of its surface in 2031.
cards.more:
A project manager compares the landing to setting down a balloon. Phobos is a rubble pile, so the ground may not hold firm.
A 23 kg, microwave-sized rover called Idefix will be released from 40 to 100 metres up, expected to bounce and self-right. Its top speed is 1 mm per second.
One scientist estimates a few hundred of the returned grains could come from Mars itself.
cards.title: Japan's MMX must touch down on a moon with almost no gravity

cards.body: Regensburg researchers sent electrons from a sharp metal tip to a silver surface a few atoms away, using laser pulses. Squeezing the timing made the electron's wave spread in space, a built-in trade-off. Much faster electronics remain a long-term goal, not a result.
cards.more:
A single atom on the surface helped confine the electron's wave packet, and simulations put its lag behind the light field at about 500 attoseconds.
An attosecond is a billionth of a billionth of a second.
The headline promise of vastly faster chips is the researchers' long-term hope. The measured finding is the trade-off itself.
cards.title: Electrons were timed at a limit set by quantum physics

cards.body: At European XFEL, a team focused hard-X-ray pulses of about 300 attoseconds onto a spot 180 by 330 nanometres. Peak intensity topped 10^20 watts per square centimetre, a record for such pulses.
cards.more:
The spot is described as about 100,000 times smaller than the cross-section of a human hair.
A thin copper sheet confirmed the intensity through the way it re-emitted X-rays.
Controlling chemistry with such pulses is a possible future goal, not something shown here.
cards.title: Europe's X-ray laser squeezed a record pulse into a tiny spot

cards.body: MD Anderson researchers found a 24-hour fast increased the microbe Akkermansia in the small intestine. Its product, propionate, made repair genes more accessible. Without the microbe, the benefit vanished. The work is preclinical; relevance to people is unknown.
cards.more:
Restoring the microbe brought the benefit back only when combined with fasting, so neither was enough alone.
The researchers suggest bacteria or their chemicals might one day give a similar effect without fasting, but that hasn't been tested.
This is lab science, not a dietary recommendation.
cards.title: In preclinical tests, a 24-hour fast primed the gut to repair itself

cards.body: MIT researchers used fat nanoparticles carrying mRNA to give natural killer cells cancer-targeting receptors while still inside the body. About 80% of the targeted cells changed. Three of five mice with aggressive melanoma had complete remission. Human safety is unknown.
cards.more:
Today's CAR therapies usually remove immune cells, edit them in a lab and return them. Doing the edit inside the body could skip that step.
The FDA has approved seven CAR T therapies in the past decade, but no CAR natural-killer therapy yet.
The team also reported cleared lymphoma tumours and healed liver damage in other mouse models.
cards.title: Nanoparticles turned immune cells into tumour hunters inside mice

cards.body: In a study of nearly 200,000 adults 65 and older, high-dose flu vaccination was linked to a nearly 55% lower Alzheimer's risk, against 40% for standard doses. The link was stronger in women. This is an association, not proof of cause.
cards.more:
Researchers could compare the two doses partly because supply shortages meant some older adults received the standard version.
The press summary doesn't spell out the study period, follow-up length or which comparison each percentage uses, so treat the numbers as rough.
The high-dose vaccine contains four times the antigen of the standard shot.
cards.title: High-dose flu shots tracked with lower Alzheimer's risk in seniors

cards.body: In a princely Scythian tomb in Tyva, researchers found about 1,000 cannabis seeds dated to the early 8th century BC. Human hair from the burial chamber held signals consistent with cannabinol, a breakdown product of THC.
cards.more:
The team calls it direct chemical evidence of psychoactive use, but the tests can't show how much was taken or how it entered the body.
The seeds probably came from wild plants, so the plants' potency is unknown.
The mound also held dozens of sacrificed horses and scattered human bones.
cards.title: Hair from a 2,800-year-old Siberian tomb carries traces of cannabis

cards.body: Durham-led researchers studied 30 teeth from 21 people buried at North Shields, England, between 1711 and 1829. Mineral defects may suggest vitamin D deficiency. Of 109 people with estimated birth years, 91 were born within a decade of a major eruption.
cards.more:
Graves were unmarked, so tooth defects couldn't be matched to individual birth dates. The analysis is community-level.
The release gives no comparison group, so the timing pattern is suggestive rather than proof.
The idea: volcanic haze and low solar output may have cut sunlight when children needed it.
cards.title: Teeth from a Quaker cemetery hint at vitamin D gaps after eruptions

cards.body: MIT engineers sewed fabric molds to cast a 3-metre beam shaped by optimization software. It used about one-third the concrete and half the steel of a conventional beam for the same load. It's a proof of concept, load-tested to about 30% of design load.
cards.more:
The team's cost analysis found fabric versions roughly 10 to 20% cheaper in the Global South, where labour costs less, but 16 to 55% pricier in the Global North because of sewing.
Only one beam has been load-tested, and it hasn't been tested to failure.
The approach suits one-off or small-batch custom elements best.
cards.title: Fabric molds made a beam with a third of the usual concrete

cards.body: Baghdad researchers put a damp cellulose pad behind a solar panel and sprayed its front when hot. In the best setup the panel ran 29.7°C cooler and about 20% more efficiently. But in the single-panel test, the pump and fan used more power than was gained.
cards.more:
Silicon panels lose about 0.5% of output per degree above 25°C, and Baghdad panels can reach around 80°C.
A KAUST researcher not involved in the study says such designs should be judged on net energy, water and cost.
The team is seeking partners for a commercial-scale pilot, where the numbers could look different.
cards.title: Wet pads cooled Baghdad solar panels by nearly 30°C

cards.body: NOAA and NASA say the 2026 Antarctic ozone hole averaged about 25 million square kilometres in peak season. They blame weather: an unusually strong polar vortex. Chlorine is down about a third since the 1980s, and recovery is still estimated by the 2070s.
cards.more:
At its peak on September 18 the hole reached about 27.1 million square kilometres, roughly 90% of the largest ever.
One expert estimates it could have been 1 to 2 million square miles bigger with year-2000 levels of ozone-depleting chemicals.
The recovery date is a scientists' estimate, not a guarantee.
cards.title: This year's ozone hole was seventh-largest in 48 years of records

cards.body: October inflation rose to 7.8% from 7.2%, with transport up 20.1%. Nomura expects the central bank to raise rates by another half point in December. The peso hit a record low of 64.17 per dollar on October 27.
cards.title: Philippine inflation hit 7.8%, its highest since early 2023

cards.body: A preprint tested six AI tools against a published review of 102 articles on a European weather pattern. The best single tool found 42 of them in initial searches. Syntheses were largely accurate but had unsupported claims and quotation errors. It hasn't been peer reviewed.
cards.more:
Library access changed results a lot: one tool went from 42 articles to 82, another from 15 to 79.
Given all 102 PDFs, three tools found every substantial article, but marked 40 to 79% of passing mentions as substantial too.
The authors tested one topic and conclude the tools help but can't replace expert judgment.
cards.title: AI tools tried to redo a literature review and fell short

cards.body: Researchers converted three open language models to read raw bytes instead of word chunks, using under 1% of the usual training data. On letter-level tasks, one converted model scored 78.1 against 54.3 for its original. General scores barely changed.
cards.more:
Part of the letter gain came from a small dose of letter-practice data, the researchers report; the byte-reading design added the rest.
The converted models were less likely to write working code on the first try.
Larger models and non-English languages weren't tested. The models, code and data were released openly.
cards.title: Teaching chatbots to read bytes made them better at spelling

cards.body: In a survey of 17,732 US adults who used cannabis in the past month, those using nearly every form had the highest rates of cannabis use disorder. It's an association from self-reports, so it can't show that mixing forms causes addiction.
cards.title: Cannabis users who mix many forms show far higher disorder rates

cards.body: That's why designs that use less concrete matter. Buildings worldwide are expected to nearly double by 2050, mostly in developing countries.

stat.label: of human-caused carbon emissions come from cement

cards.title: Cement is behind roughly 8% of human-caused carbon emissions

beats: Immune cells recognize threats using receptors, proteins on their surface that fit specific targets.
A CAR, or chimeric antigen receptor, is a lab-designed receptor that locks onto a chosen marker on cancer cells.
Standard treatment removes a patient's T cells, adds the CAR gene outside the body, and infuses them back.
Natural killer cells are another type of immune cell, and they may be simpler to use.
Newer research delivers mRNA instructions directly inside the body, so the cell builds its CAR in place.
cards.title: How a CAR gives an immune cell new eyes

beats: Most language models don't read letters; they read tokens, which are common chunks of text.
A word like 'strawberry' may arrive as a couple of chunks, each turned into a number.
The model never directly sees the individual letters inside those chunks.
So counting the r's means reasoning about spelling it was never shown directly.
Reading raw bytes instead gives the model the actual characters, at the cost of more steps.
cards.title: Why chatbots stumble when counting the letters in a word

beats: A logarithm asks: what power do I raise a base to, to get this number?
In base 10, the log of 1,000 is 3, because 10 × 10 × 10 is 1,000.
Every step up the scale multiplies the real amount by the same factor.
That's why earthquake magnitudes, decibels and pH all use log scales.
One magnitude step on an earthquake scale means about 32 times more energy.
cards.title: Logarithms: how one number can span a huge range

beats: Countries buy many essentials, like oil, from abroad, usually priced in dollars.
If your currency weakens, the same barrel costs more in local money.
Higher fuel costs then spread into transport, food and electricity bills.
Central banks may raise interest rates to make holding their currency more attractive.
The trade-off: dearer loans can also slow spending and growth at home.
cards.title: How a falling currency pushes up prices at home

beats: Ozone high in the atmosphere absorbs much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light.
In the dark Antarctic winter, a ring of winds called the polar vortex seals off cold air.
Extremely cold clouds form there and turn chlorine from old chemicals into reactive forms.
When sunlight returns in spring, that chlorine rapidly destroys ozone.
As the vortex breaks up in late spring, ozone-rich air flows back in and the hole closes.
cards.title: Why the ozone hole opens over Antarctica each spring

beats: Storytellers can report thoughts directly: 'She thought, I will not cry.'
Free indirect speech drops the 'she thought' and slips into the character's voice.
'She would not cry. Not here, not in front of him.'
The narrator's words now carry the character's feelings, blurring whose view we're in.
Jane Austen used it to let readers enjoy a character's blind spots from inside.
cards.title: Free indirect speech: when a narrator thinks like a character

myth.claim: One half of the Moon never sees the Sun.
myth.truth: Every part of the Moon gets about two weeks of daylight a month. The far side is only hidden from Earth, because the Moon turns once for each orbit. It's 'far', not 'dark'.

cards.title: The far side of the Moon is always dark

myth.claim: Einstein flunked math at school.
myth.truth: He had mastered calculus by about 15 and denied the rumour himself. At 16 he did fail an entrance exam for a Zurich college, but did very well in maths and physics; other subjects let him down.

cards.title: Einstein failed math as a student

myth.claim: The color red makes bulls angry.
myth.truth: Cattle are essentially red-blind, with color vision built on only two cone types. What provokes the charge is the cape's motion. A matador's red cape is tradition, not provocation.

cards.title: Bulls charge because they hate red

quiz.q: A patch of lilies doubles daily and covers a pond on day 30. When was it half covered?
quiz.why: It doubles each day, so half-covered is exactly one doubling before full: day 29. Exponential growth looks small until the very end.

cards.title: Lilies on a pond: when is it half covered?

quiz.q: What does the word 'disaster' literally mean?
quiz.why: From Italian 'disastro': 'dis-' (bad) plus 'astro' (star). An unlucky event was blamed on an ill-starred sky.

cards.title: The star hiding inside the word 'disaster'

cards.body: Using preview data covering about 7% of the sky, the Rubin Observatory spotted Aquarius IV, a faint galaxy roughly 355,000 light-years away, and Rubin-GC1, a star cluster hidden behind thick dust. About 65 Milky Way satellite galaxies are known; some estimates say hundreds remain.
cards.more:
Rubin sits on Cerro Pachón in Chile and uses an 8.4-metre telescope with a 3.2-gigapixel camera.
The data behind these finds was gathered between April 2025 and January 2026, before the main 10-year survey began.
Counting faint satellite galaxies is a test of dark-matter theories, which predict how many small clumps should orbit a big galaxy.
cards.title: Rubin found two hidden neighbours of the Milky Way in its first data

cards.body: ESO's Very Large Telescope found the white dwarf J1328−1450 circled by two debris rings with a gap between them. The inner ring is rich in magnesium gas; the outer one lacks it. Astronomers suspect two unseen surviving bodies, one possibly Pluto- or Moon-sized, are sculpting the rings.
cards.more:
White dwarfs are the cooling cores left when stars like the Sun die. Rocky bodies that stray too close get torn apart, and their dust forms discs.
The team detected calcium, oxygen, magnesium and iron, which hints at what the destroyed worlds were made of.
The two shepherding bodies have not been seen directly; their existence is inferred from the rings' shape. The study is in Nature Astronomy.
cards.title: A dead star wears two rings of shattered planets

cards.body: NASA's November sky guide: the Leonids are best before dawn on November 17 and 18, at up to about 15 meteors an hour in ideal dark skies. Mars and Jupiter sit about 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise on November 15 and 16. A full supermoon follows on November 24.
cards.more:
The November 24 supermoon is the first of three in a row.
The Northern Taurids also peak around November 12, but at only about five meteors an hour.
Real meteor counts are usually lower than the ideal figures, especially near cities.
cards.title: Leonid meteors, a Mars–Jupiter pairing and a supermoon this month

cards.body: A team at Germany's University of Würzburg isolated stable oxoboranes, molecules with a triple bond between boron and oxygen that chemists have chased since at least the early 1960s. Two doctoral students hit on it by reacting a boron compound with ketones, yielding orange and yellow solids.
cards.more:
Such bonds are normally so reactive that the molecules fall apart or clump together almost instantly.
The team has now made three different oxoboranes, with computer modelling support from Tezpur University in India. The paper is in Nature Chemistry.
The researchers are still testing how widely the method works.
cards.title: Chemists finally made a boron–oxygen triple bond stay put

cards.body: In US adults followed for up to 43 years, people drinking more caffeinated coffee had 141 dementia cases per 100,000 a year, versus 330 among those who rarely drank it. The link peaked at two to three cups. Decaf showed no link, and this is a correlation, not proof.
cards.more:
For tea, the strongest association was at one to two cups a day, though the study didn't separate caffeinated from caffeine-free tea.
The link held regardless of genetic risk. Self-reported memory slips were also a little less common: 7.8% versus 9.5%.
Coffee drinkers may differ in other ways that matter, so the researchers do not claim coffee prevents dementia. Published in JAMA.
cards.title: Two to three cups of coffee a day tracked with lower dementia rates

cards.body: UC Santa Cruz researchers watched neurons in living mice and saw a burst of new dendritic spines, the tiny contact points between cells, within 24 hours of psilocybin. In stressed mice, it also halted unusually fast loss of connections. One serotonin receptor type proved necessary for the effect.
cards.more:
In healthy mice, the extra connections drifted back toward normal over three weeks.
The key was serotonin 2A receptors on one class of neuron in the cortex. Mice lacking those receptors there still showed the drug's usual head-twitch reaction, suggesting the rewiring and that reaction can be separated.
This was mouse work; whether the same happens in people needs more research. Published in Nature Neuroscience.
cards.title: In mice, psilocybin sprouted new brain connections within a day

cards.body: Swinburne University researchers found sulforaphane, a compound in broccoli, raised levels of frataxin in nerve cells grown from stem cells. People with Friedreich ataxia, a rare inherited nerve disease with no cure, lack enough frataxin. The work is preclinical; trials in patients haven't happened yet.
cards.more:
Sulforaphane also seemed to protect the vulnerable sensory nerve cells from damage in the lab.
It already has a known safety record in children and adults, which could speed testing. The team is seeking funding for clinical trials.
Eating broccoli is not a treatment: lab doses and dietary amounts are very different things.
cards.title: A broccoli compound boosted a missing protein in lab-grown nerve cells

cards.body: NC State researchers identified the root-chewing larvae as a longhorn beetle, Prionus imbricornis, whose grubs can reach five inches. Pheromone traps and DNA barcoding at six farms confirmed it. No insecticide is currently labelled for this pest in blueberries.
cards.more:
Growers had reported mystery grubs damaging blueberry roots since 2010.
North Carolina is the first state to document this beetle feeding on blueberry bushes.
The team is now testing treatments timed to the beetle's breeding cycle. The study is in the Journal of Integrated Pest Management.
cards.title: Five-inch beetle grubs are eating North Carolina's blueberry roots

cards.body: An Aarhus University review argues that for more than 20 million years Europe was mostly open woodland and meadow, kept that way by elephants, rhinos, aurochs and bison. Evidence spans fossil pollen, charcoal, insect fossils, chemical clues in teeth and ancient DNA.
cards.more:
The review covers the Miocene, from about 23 million years ago, up to pre-industrial times.
The authors say this challenges the idea that Europe's natural state is closed forest.
They argue that subsidies for planting dense forest, as in Denmark, may hurt biodiversity. That is their recommendation, published in Biological Conservation.
cards.title: Europe's wild past was open woodland and grazers, not dense forest

cards.body: Bournemouth University's Miles Russell argues Verica, ruler of the Atrebates tribe whose ousting in AD 40 helped trigger Rome's invasion, was female. He points to a name ending like Boudicca's, coins showing a feminine rider, and the Latin title rex, which he says isn't gender-specific.
cards.more:
Verica fled to Emperor Claudius after being driven out, and Rome invaded Britain three years later.
Russell notes Cleopatra also used the title rex. Verica's gold coins carry the letters VIR and REX.
This is one researcher's interpretation, and it challenges a long-held assumption.
cards.title: An archaeologist argues Iron Age Britain's King Verica was a woman

cards.body: Mathematician Miloslav Druckmüller's team shot the August 2026 total eclipse from Spain with eight cameras, each filtered to a narrow colour emitted by charged iron in the Sun's corona. Each final image draws on about 3,000 frames and over two days of processing.
cards.more:
Totality lasted 107 seconds at their site, during which they took about 200 exposures per image.
The corona's brightness can range by perhaps a million to one, while a monitor shows around 800 to one, so algorithms must compress that range without losing detail.
The iron-line images, which map the corona's temperature, may take months or even a year to finish.
cards.title: One eclipse photo can take 3,000 frames and two days of computing

cards.body: MIT and BASF researchers built CheMeleon, a model pre-trained on about a million PubChem molecules, then fine-tuned for tasks like predicting toxicity or solubility. Across 58 tests, the authors say it beat other models. It's open source.
cards.more:
The pre-training taught it about 1,600 descriptors chemists already use, so it needs fewer lab measurements for each new problem.
The team says nine of the top 20 entries in a drug-property prediction contest used it. Those are the researchers' claims.
The paper appeared in the Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling.
cards.title: An AI pre-trained on a million molecules predicts from scant data

cards.body: MIT's UQ-DAAAM lets a robot score how unsure it is about each object it has labelled in its 3D map, then re-check doubtful ones from more viewpoints. That fixed ambiguities for about 92% of objects, and the authors report a 5% accuracy gain over the previous best.
cards.more:
It combines the vision-language model's own confidence with how consistent captions are across different views.
In one example, a grey chimney first labelled a squirrel was corrected.
The work will be presented at NeurIPS; the figures are the researchers' reported results.
cards.title: A robot learned to doubt its labels after calling a chimney a squirrel

cards.body: A University of Bath model finds the CO2 from human metabolism rose 74% from 1985 to 2015, mostly from population growth. The authors stress it isn't driving climate change: breath carbon cycles through food, unlike fossil carbon.
cards.more:
More than 60% of the increase came from population growth alone.
The team combined thousands of metabolic measurements with population and body-weight data. Published in The Lancet Planetary Health.
cards.title: Humanity's breathing now releases about 2 billion tonnes of CO2 a year

cards.body: The visible surface is only about 5,500 °C. Why the corona is so much hotter is still an open question, which is one reason scientists photograph it during eclipses.

stat.label: Rough temperature of the Sun's corona

cards.title: The Sun's thin outer halo is far hotter than its surface

beats: A foundation model is first trained on a huge, general dataset before it ever sees your specific problem.
That pre-training teaches broad patterns, like how words relate or how molecular shapes affect behaviour.
Fine-tuning then adjusts the model on a small, task-specific dataset, such as a few hundred toxicity measurements.
Because the basics are already learned, the model needs far fewer new examples to do well.
MIT's CheMeleon applies this to chemistry, pre-training on about a million molecules.
cards.title: What a foundation model is, and why it needs less data

beats: A confounder is something that influences both the thing you're studying and the outcome.
Ice cream sales and drownings rise together, but hot weather drives both.
In health studies, coffee drinkers might also differ in income, sleep or exercise.
Researchers adjust for known confounders statistically, but unknown ones can still lurk.
That's why observational links, like coffee and dementia, are called associations, not proof.
cards.title: How a hidden third factor can fake a cause

beats: The nominal return is the headline rate, say 5% a year on a deposit.
Inflation measures how much prices rise, shrinking what each rupee or dollar buys.
The real return is roughly the nominal return minus inflation.
Earn 5% while prices climb 6%, and your money buys about 1% less after a year.
So a 'safe' account can quietly lose ground if its rate trails inflation.
cards.title: Your real return is what's left after inflation

beats: Act one sets up the hero's ordinary world and ends with an event that disrupts it.
Act two, usually the longest, raises the stakes through obstacles and rising complications.
Midway, a turn often changes what the hero wants or understands.
Act three brings the climax, where the central conflict is finally faced.
It's a guide, not a law: many great stories bend or break it deliberately.
cards.title: The three-act structure behind most stories you love

beats: Plants pull CO2 from the air and lock its carbon into sugars and tissues.
When we eat those plants, or animals that ate them, our bodies burn that carbon and exhale it.
That breath simply returns carbon taken from the air months or years earlier.
Fossil fuels release carbon that sat underground for millions of years.
That's extra carbon added to the cycle, which is what raises atmospheric CO2.
cards.title: Why your breath doesn't warm the planet but a car's exhaust does

beats: The Moon's orbit is an oval, so its distance from Earth keeps changing.
Its closest point each orbit is called perigee; the farthest is apogee.
A supermoon is a full moon that happens near perigee.
It can look up to about 14% bigger and 30% brighter than a full moon at apogee.
Without a side-by-side comparison, most people can't spot the size difference by eye.
cards.title: What makes a full moon a 'supermoon'

myth.claim: Glass is a very slow liquid, so centuries-old panes have sagged and thickened at the bottom.
myth.truth: Glass is an amorphous solid. At room temperature its flow is far too slow to notice over centuries. Old panes were uneven from how they were made, and glaziers often set the thicker edge at the bottom.

cards.title: Old church windows are thick at the bottom because glass flows

myth.claim: Getting a raise that crosses into a higher tax bracket means all your income gets taxed more, so you take home less.
myth.truth: In marginal tax systems, only the income above the threshold is taxed at the higher rate. A raise alone doesn't lower take-home pay through income tax, though losing an income-based benefit can occasionally do so.

cards.title: A raise can push you into a higher bracket and shrink your pay

myth.claim: 'Sincere' comes from Latin 'sine cera', meaning 'without wax', describing honest sculptors who didn't hide cracks with wax.
myth.truth: It's a charming folk etymology with no ancient evidence. The word comes from Latin 'sincerus', meaning clean, pure or whole; its deeper origin is uncertain.

cards.title: 'Sincere' comes from sculptures sold 'without wax'

quiz.q: Which Roman emperor launched the invasion of Britain in AD 43?
quiz.why: Claudius ordered the invasion, partly after the ousted British ruler Verica fled to him asking for help.

cards.title: Who sent Rome's legions to conquer Britain in AD 43?

quiz.why: Pair the ends: 1+100, 2+99 and so on each make 101. There are 50 pairs, so 50 × 101 = 5,050.

cards.title: Add 1 to 100 in your head with one trick

quiz.q: The word 'galaxy' comes from a Greek word for what?
quiz.why: Greek 'gala' means milk; our own galaxy looks like a milky band across the night sky, hence the Milky Way.

cards.title: The drink hiding inside the word 'galaxy'

quiz.q: After a year, what can your savings buy compared with before?
quiz.why: Your balance grew 2%, but prices grew 3%, so its real buying power fell by roughly 1%.

cards.title: Your savings earn 2% while prices rise 3%. What happened?

cards.body: Chemists found mineralized red blood cells in the limb bones of Aratasaurus, a meat-eating dinosaur from northeastern Brazil. The cells still held traces of heme, the iron-carrying part of hemoglobin, which the team calls the first definitive chemical confirmation of its kind.
cards.more:
The cells sat inside tiny canals that once carried blood through the bone.
The animal was probably buried quickly in oxygen-poor sediment full of microbes, and a manganese mineral called hausmannite seems to have helped lock the molecules in place.
The team, led by Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Australia, also detected amino acids linked to collagen. The study is in PNAS.
cards.title: Red blood cells survived inside a 115-million-year-old dinosaur

cards.body: Swift, launched in 2004 to catch gamma-ray bursts, fell back to Earth this week over North Sumatra, Indonesia. Planned for two years, it worked more than ten times longer, swinging its three telescopes toward cosmic explosions within moments and alerting observatories worldwide.
cards.more:
The US Space Force confirmed the re-entry at 7:39 a.m. EST. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some parts may have survived.
Beyond gamma-ray bursts, Swift studied black-hole-powered galaxies, flaring stars, supernovae, and comets and asteroids closer to home.
cards.title: NASA's Swift telescope burned up after nearly 22 years in orbit

cards.body: White dwarfs are thought to max out near 1.4 times the Sun's mass. Simulations from the Indian Institute of Science suggest strong internal magnetic fields could prop one up to about 2.4 solar masses. That could explain some unusually bright stellar explosions.
cards.more:
The team added magnetic fields and cooling to STARS, a stellar evolution code first built at Cambridge. Without magnetism, the same model topped out around 1.4 solar masses.
Some Type Ia supernovae, which come from exploding white dwarfs, look too bright for a normal-mass star. Magnetic pressure might also explain why some white dwarfs look larger than models predict.
These are computer results, not observations. The paper is in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
cards.title: Strong magnetism might let dead stars blow past their weight limit

cards.body: ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter keeps detecting hydrogen chloride over Alba Mons, Mars's largest volcano by area, in early northern summer. Researchers mapped fracture networks there and suggest gas trapped in winter ice escapes as it warms. The volcano was thought dead for about 3.2 billion years.
cards.more:
Over two Martian years the team logged eight confident detections in 78 relevant observations, peaking around 1.5 parts per billion.
Cameras on the orbiter and NASA's HiRISE revealed cracks from tens of centimetres wide to kilometres long.
The article reports the study in Science Advances. Whether the gas points to underground magma today is still an open question.
cards.title: A gas seeping near a huge Martian volcano hints at deep heat

cards.body: Scientists read proteins from the enamel of six Homo erectus teeth from three Chinese sites. One protein variant is shared with Denisovans, hinting the two groups interbred in East Asia. A matching variant survives in about 21% of people in the Philippines today.
cards.more:
All six teeth also share a variant seen in no other human relative, which confirms the fossils from Hexian belong to Homo erectus.
One reading is that the variant passed from erectus to Denisovans, and later from Denisovans into ancestors of Southeast Asians and Oceanians. In India it is about 1%.
No one yet knows what the variant does. The study, led by Qiaomei Fu, is in Nature.
cards.title: Proteins in 400,000-year-old teeth link Homo erectus to Denisovans

cards.body: Divers off Takashima Island investigated a third wreck from the failed Yuan dynasty invasion of 1281. The roughly 100-foot ship, likely a mother ship with living quarters, held five dice and 29 small cards for koppai, a Chinese game seen as an ancestor of mahjong.
cards.more:
Two earlier wrecks from the same fleet were found in 2011 and 2015.
Kokugakuin University's Yoshifumi Ikeda, who led the work with the Matsuura city government, says the cards were probably for off-duty fun.
cards.title: Playing cards found in a ship from the 1281 Mongol invasion of Japan

cards.body: At Old Dongola in Sudan, a Sudanese-Polish team uncovered a grand staircase and, for the first time, the original floor of the Great Church of Jesus. The church of the Christian kingdom of Makuria was about 47 m wide and 57 m long, with walls still 11 m high.
cards.more:
Its height is estimated at about 21 metres. A smaller church built on top yielded so much painted plaster that the team needs six large shelving units for it, including Greek biblical texts.
The dig is led by Artur Obłuski of the University of Warsaw with Sudan's antiquities authority. Floods in 2024 damaged some protective roofs.
cards.title: Diggers reached the floor of medieval Nubia's biggest church

cards.body: A US trial of 5,772 people compared choosing statins by a standard risk score or by a coronary calcium scan. After about four years, 2.7% of each group had a major heart event. Calcium-scan patients got far fewer statin recommendations but were more likely to take them.
cards.more:
The risk-score group was told to take statins more than three times as often. Yet among those advised, 62% of the scan group stuck with the pills versus 23% of the score group.
The trial saw fewer events than expected, so it could not prove the two approaches are equivalent. The investigators call the results hypothesis-generating. It was presented at ESC Congress 2026.
cards.title: Artery scans and risk scores tied for heart outcomes in a big trial

cards.body: In a University of Toronto trial, 74 adults with overweight or obesity ate either little dairy or three daily servings. The dairy groups showed no meaningful differences in weight, body fat or cholesterol, and their blood pressure improved. The study was small and short.
cards.more:
The dairy eaters also took in more calcium, protein and vitamin D, with no sign of insulin resistance.
Three months cannot show long-term effects on diabetes or heart disease. The work was partly funded by a dairy research program, and it appears in The Journal of Nutrition.
cards.title: Daily full-fat dairy didn't add weight in a 12-week trial

cards.body: Healthy adults aged 45 to 65 took a low daily dose of rapamycin for four weeks. Brain blood flow rose in carriers of APOE4, a gene variant linked to Alzheimer's risk, but not in non-carriers. Women carriers improved most.
cards.more:
This was a small pilot study at the University of Missouri. It did not test whether rapamycin prevents Alzheimer's or protects memory.
Rapamycin is normally used to prevent organ transplant rejection. Earlier mouse work by the same lead, Ai-Ling Lin, prompted the trial.
cards.title: A low-dose transplant drug boosted brain blood flow in APOE4 carriers

cards.body: KAIST and Georgia Tech researchers found that crude oil gunking up a porous plastic membrane shrinks its pores below 2 nanometres, letting it sieve oil fractions without boiling. Lab flow rates were about 23 times past membranes. Simulations suggest refining could use about a third less energy.
cards.more:
Refineries normally heat crude above 350 °C to separate it. The membrane ran stably for 28 days in the lab on real crude.
The projected savings, such as 31.6% less energy and 37.6% less CO2, come from simulations, not working refineries. The study is in Nature.
cards.title: A filter clogged by crude oil turned out to sort oil better

cards.body: Oak Ridge researchers pressed tiny crystals of manganese telluride and iron sulfide between titanium plates. Neutron scans showed the strain shifted which magnetic domains dominated and changed how current flowed. Both are altermagnets, a recently confirmed third kind of magnetism.
cards.more:
Altermagnets have no overall magnetic pull, like antiferromagnets, yet their electrons behave in direction-dependent ways, like in ferromagnets.
Being able to tune them by squeezing could help spintronics, which stores data in electron spin. The results are in Physical Review X and Advanced Materials.
cards.title: A gentle squeeze rearranges magnetism in a new class of magnets

cards.body: The EU now requires AI-written text to be marked. Tests of OpenAI's textGrain watermark caught about 80% of 150-word texts and 95% of 300-word ones. Swapping 10% of words for synonyms cut detection from 92% to 66%, by OpenAI's own figures.
cards.more:
Replacing up to a quarter of the words dropped detection to 17%. OpenAI reports a 1% false-positive rate.
The EU AI Act's transparency rules took effect on 2 August. OpenAI says textGrain matched or beat Google's SynthID Text, a claim not yet independently checked.
cards.title: OpenAI's text watermark weakens on short or edited text

cards.body: London firm Samphire Neuroscience says its headband, which sends a weak current through the scalp, is now approved in the UK and EU for anxiety symptoms of PMDD, a severe form of PMS. An independent 42-person study, not yet published, found less anxiety but no change in depressive symptoms.
cards.more:
The device was already approved there for period pain and PMS. The study used one 20-minute session a day for two weeks before each period.
Minor skin burns under the electrodes are the main reported side effect of home devices like this. Anyone considering one should talk to a doctor.
cards.title: A home brain-stimulation headband won approval for PMDD anxiety

cards.body: US employers added 165,000 jobs in October and unemployment dipped to 4.1%. Hourly pay rose 3.1% over a year, yet wages have lagged inflation for seven straight months. Traders now see about a 77% chance of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December.
cards.more:
Economists had expected about 65,000 new jobs. Professional and business services led with 70,000, while hotels, restaurants and bars shed about 10,600.
GDP grew at a 3.4% annual pace in the third quarter, and higher gasoline prices are adding to inflation.
cards.title: US hiring beat forecasts, but pay is still trailing prices

cards.body: Average monthly US job growth has picked up sharply since 2025, and October's gain was more than double what economists expected.
cards.title: October's US job gains dwarfed recent averages

cards.body: Refineries heat crude above 350 °C so its parts boil off at different temperatures. That heating step is one of the most energy-hungry jobs in industry, which is why filters that sort oil without boiling it draw so much interest.

stat.label: used each year worldwide just to distill crude oil

cards.title: Boiling crude oil apart takes a staggering amount of energy

beats: A wave function gives the odds of each outcome, like 77% red and 23% green.
One camp says it is only our knowledge, like odds on a coin already lying under a cup.
In 2012, Pusey, Barrett and Rudolph proved a theorem now called PBR.
Under modest assumptions, two different wave functions can never describe the same hidden reality.
So if a hidden reality exists, the wave function must be part of it, not mere ignorance.
cards.more:
The theorem builds on Einstein's 1935 EPR argument and John Bell's 1964 result.
Researchers including a Cambridge-led team have since tested PBR-style games on quantum computers.
Some physicists respond by dropping the idea of an observer-independent reality altogether, as in QBism.
cards.title: Is the quantum wave function real, or just our ignorance?

beats: A white dwarf is the hot, Earth-sized core left after a Sun-like star dies.
Gravity tries to crush it, and nothing is burning inside to push back.
Instead, electrons packed tightly resist being squeezed further, a quantum effect called degeneracy pressure.
Past about 1.4 Suns of mass, gravity wins; this is the Chandrasekhar limit.
A white dwarf pushed past it can explode as a Type Ia supernova.
cards.more:
Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar worked out the limit around 1930 and later shared the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Because these explosions are fairly uniform, astronomers use them as distance markers, which is why a possible heavier, magnetized white dwarf matters.
cards.title: Why a white dwarf star has a maximum weight

beats: A language model picks each next word from many plausible options.
A watermark uses a secret key to nudge those picks toward certain words.
Readers can't notice, but a detector holding the key counts the favoured words.
Too many favoured words to be chance means the text is likely machine-made.
Short or reworded text gives fewer clues, so the signal fades.
cards.more:
This is why detection rates climb with length: each word adds a little statistical evidence.
Watermarks only work if the model's maker builds them in; text from models without one carries no such mark.
cards.title: How you hide a watermark inside ordinary sentences

beats: The US jobs report comes from two surveys: one of employers, one of households.
The employer survey counts jobs added; the household survey gives the unemployment rate.
The rate is jobless people actively seeking work divided by everyone working or seeking.
If new job-seekers mostly land jobs, the rate can drop while the labour force grows.
People who stop looking leave the count, which can flatter the rate.
cards.more:
That's why economists also watch the participation rate, the share of adults working or looking for work.
The two surveys can disagree month to month, and both get revised later.
cards.title: How unemployment can fall even as more people look for work

beats: A study's result is an estimate, and a different sample would give a slightly different number.
A 95% confidence interval is a range built to capture the true value 95% of the time.
A hazard ratio of 1 means no difference in risk between two groups.
In the statin trial, the interval ran from 0.71 to 1.38, spanning both better and worse.
A wide interval means 'we can't tell yet', not 'they're the same'.
cards.more:
More participants or more events shrink the interval, which is why trials aim for large numbers.
Absence of evidence for a difference is not evidence of no difference.
cards.title: What a confidence interval is really telling you

beats: Telling states a feeling outright: 'She was nervous.'
Showing gives evidence: she checked her ticket for the fifth time.
Readers who work out the feeling themselves tend to feel it more.
But showing everything is slow, so writers summarise the dull stretches.
Good rule of thumb: show the moments that matter, tell the ones that connect them.
cards.more:
The advice is common in writing workshops and screenwriting, where action must carry emotion on screen.
Overdone, it produces purple prose; used well, it lets readers do the satisfying work of inference.
cards.title: 'Show, don't tell', and when telling is the right call

myth.claim: Logical people are left-brain dominant and creative people are right-brain dominant.
myth.truth: Some tasks lean on one hemisphere, like language on the left for most people. But a 2013 University of Utah study of over 1,000 brain scans found no evidence that individuals use one whole side more. Both hemispheres work together constantly.

cards.title: Left-brained versus right-brained people

myth.claim: Goldfish forget everything after about three seconds.
myth.truth: Goldfish can learn to respond to sounds, colours and feeding times, and remember them for months. Researchers have trained them to push levers and navigate simple mazes.

cards.title: The three-second goldfish

myth.claim: 'Irregardless' is not a real word.
myth.truth: It has been in use for over a century and major dictionaries list it, labelled nonstandard. It likely blends 'irrespective' and 'regardless'. It is a real word, just one that many editors and teachers dislike; 'regardless' is the safer choice in formal writing.

cards.title: 'Irregardless' isn't a word

quiz.q: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 together. The bat costs $1.00 more than the ball. What does the ball cost?
quiz.why: If the ball were 10 cents, the bat would be $1.10 and the total $1.20. Ball 5 cents plus bat $1.05 gives $1.10.

cards.title: The bat-and-ball trap

quiz.q: Measured from its base to its summit, which mountain is tallest?
quiz.why: Hawaii's Mauna Kea rises about 10,200 m from the sea floor, though only about 4,200 m is above sea level. Everest is highest above sea level at 8,849 m.

cards.title: Which mountain is tallest from base to peak?

quiz.q: The word 'muscle' comes from a Latin word meaning what?
quiz.why: Latin 'musculus' means little mouse; a flexing muscle under the skin reminded Romans of a mouse moving.

cards.title: The animal hiding in the word 'muscle'

cards.body: On October 11, NASA's Perseverance rover passed 45.22 km (28.1 miles) of total driving on Mars, a record recognized by Guinness. Engineers got there by letting it tilt more steeply and navigate itself by matching ground photos to orbital maps.
cards.more:
The rover had been about 200 m short earlier but stopped to study rocks before claiming the record.
One upgrade lets it work out where it is by comparing its own camera images with pictures taken from orbit, so it needs less help from Earth.
The extra computer it uses for this needed software protection against radiation flipping bits in memory. NASA says it is also exploring generative AI for route planning, but that is not in use yet.
cards.title: Perseverance has now driven farther than any vehicle on another world

cards.body: Deep-sleep slow waves normally sweep across the brain together. A Berkeley team found that older adults with more tau protein in the frontal cortex had shorter, more isolated waves, and they recalled fewer word pairs the next morning.
cards.more:
The study, in Nature Neuroscience, combined sleep EEG with PET brain scans and compared young adults with people in their mid-60s to mid-70s.
In people followed for several years, rising tau came with less coordinated waves and worse overnight memory.
The authors stress this is a correlation: it does not prove tau causes the memory loss or that the waves are the mechanism. Some participants with tau were cognitively normal for their age.
cards.title: 'Lonely' sleep waves track tau buildup and weaker overnight memory

cards.body: Nottingham researchers made a fluoride-free protein gel that seeps into enamel microcracks and uses calcium and phosphate from saliva to grow new, aligned crystals. In lab tests mimicking brushing and acidic food, the new layer behaved much like healthy enamel.
cards.more:
Enamel normally cannot repair itself because the cells that make it are gone once a tooth erupts. The gel mimics the proteins that guide enamel growth in childhood.
It also formed an enamel-like coat over exposed dentine, the softer layer underneath.
These are lab results only; long-term performance in real mouths is untested. A spin-out company is developing it and hopes for a first product soon.
cards.title: A lab-made gel coaxed tooth enamel to regrow in the lab

cards.body: An international guideline in Nature Medicine sets out more than 60 recommendations for phage therapy: using viruses that infect bacteria to treat drug-resistant infections. It covers picking, testing, making and giving the phages, but does not endorse routine use.
cards.more:
It was drafted by 20 professional bodies, 18 experts including regulators, and two patient groups, led by German infectious-disease specialists.
In one Belgian series of 100 patients, 77% improved and the target bacteria became undetectable in 61%. That series had no control group, so it cannot show the phages caused the recovery.
Controlled trials are still needed to show how reliably the treatment works.
cards.title: Doctors now have a rulebook for treating superbugs with viruses

cards.body: Stanford's Peptide Predictor narrowed about 20,000 human genes to 373 hormone precursors and flagged a tiny 12-amino-acid peptide called BRP. In mice and minipigs, one dose cut food intake by up to half over the next hour.
cards.more:
In obese mice dosed daily for 14 days, treated animals lost about 3 g, mostly fat, while untreated ones gained about 3 g.
In lab-grown neurons, BRP boosted activity about tenfold, compared with threefold for GLP-1, the hormone that drugs like Ozempic mimic.
This is animal work only. Human safety, side effects like nausea, and even which receptor BRP acts on are still unknown. The lead scientist co-founded a company developing it.
cards.title: An algorithm sifted 20,000 genes and found an appetite-cutting peptide

cards.body: MIT chemists joined nanoparticles with flexible polymer strands tipped with opposite charges, instead of the usual rigid links. Changing particle size and strand length produced open, previously unseen crystal arrangements of particles.
cards.more:
For about two decades, nanoparticle crystals were mostly built with stiff connectors, which limits how particles can pack.
With flexible linkers, how many neighbours each particle bonds to depends on charge and flexibility, opening new geometries.
The team, publishing in Nature Materials, says uses in optics, catalysis and energy are possible but need more development.
cards.title: Floppy, charged links built never-before-seen nanoparticle crystals

cards.body: Physicists in Brazil and China propose reading a superconducting qubit by measuring the tiny current it drives around a superconducting loop, sensed by a nearby SQUID. In noisy simulations, readout accuracy reached up to 99.85%.
cards.more:
Reading a qubit usually means coupling it to extra helper qubits, which adds complexity and errors.
Here the current oscillates with no applied voltage, and its offset, size and timing encode the qubit's state.
The work, in Physical Review B, is purely theoretical. The device geometry has not been built yet.
cards.title: A proposed way to read a qubit by listening to its supercurrent

cards.body: A Texas A&M analysis pooled 50,000 correlations from 137 test batteries. Picking out the sounds inside words and knowing vocabulary and background facts were the most reliable predictors of reading ability; visual processing showed no meaningful link.
cards.more:
General intelligence was linked to reading, but less strongly than some earlier reviews suggested. Memory, reasoning and processing speed played supporting roles.
This is a synthesis of correlations, so it shows what goes together, not what causes reading success.
The paper appeared in the Journal of Intelligence.
cards.title: Hearing sounds in words and knowing words predict reading best

cards.body: Metal-organic frameworks are sponge-like crystals that can be melted into glass. German and UK chemists added a molecule called phenanthroline before melting; it lowered the melting point and bonded to the metal atoms, rewiring the glass's structure.
cards.more:
The amount added controls how much the structure changes, giving a dial for tuning the material.
Gentler melting also avoided unwanted breakdown products in cobalt-based glasses.
The study is in Nature Materials. Uses in catalysts, sensors, batteries and gas storage are possibilities, not demonstrations.
cards.title: A helper molecule lets chemists reshape a new kind of glass

cards.body: Residents in a Baton Rouge neighbourhood say Amazon's delivery drones have buzzed overhead almost nonstop since September; one counted a drone every 48 seconds. As drone firms plan huge expansions, towns and states are pushing back.
cards.more:
The drones fly from a site about 3 km away. An FAA environmental review allows up to 1,000 deliveries a day there.
Amazon aims to serve 500 municipalities by end of 2026, and other firms plan hundreds of hubs. In September, 15 states sued the FAA over easing environmental review.
Who controls the low airspace over private homes is still legally unsettled.
cards.title: Delivery drones are bringing a new noise complaint to US suburbs

cards.body: French archaeologists excavated a Neolithic cemetery at Champigny-sur-Marne with 11 graves and 30 megaliths. Its centrepiece is a toppled, human-shaped menhir weighing over 9 tonnes that once stood more than 3 m tall, possibly painted.
cards.more:
The stone has a carved belt, an arc of small cup-shaped hollows, and faint white and black stains that may be pigment.
Most graves had a post hole near the head. One held an adult buried seated, legs encased in mineral deposits.
The dig was run by Inrap, France's preventive archaeology institute.
cards.title: A 6,500-year-old human-shaped standing stone found near Paris

cards.body: A brass combination lock recovered off Wales was scanned with micro-CT, revealing its hidden mechanism. A Cardiff University researcher matched the notches to letters and found the four-letter code: ANCE.
cards.more:
The wreck is thought to be the Ann Frances, an English merchant ship lost in a storm in 1583.
The lock lay near Spanish silver coins and probably secured a small chest of valuables that has not survived.
The ship's identity and the chest's contents are interpretations, and the work has not yet appeared in a journal.
cards.title: X-ray scans cracked the code of a lock from a 1583 shipwreck

cards.body: On November 5 the Bank of England lifted its key rate from 3.75% to 4%. Eight of nine policymakers voted for the move, and the one dissenter wanted a bigger hike. Governor Andrew Bailey said more rises may follow if energy prices stay high.
cards.more:
Markets had not fully expected a split in favour of a larger rise.
Two-year UK government bond yields edged up after the decision, and traders priced in more tightening by the end of 2027.
Raising rates makes borrowing dearer, which cools spending and, over time, inflation.
cards.title: The Bank of England raised rates for the first time in three years

cards.body: Most come from the Sun's core and pass straight through you, and the whole Earth, almost never touching an atom. IceCube in Antarctica uses a cubic kilometre of ice to catch a few dozen of the most energetic ones a year.
cards.more:
Some of IceCube's catches carry around 10 billion times the energy of a typical solar neutrino; where they come from is still unknown.
The detector watches for faint blue flashes when a rare neutrino does hit something in the ice.

stat.label: neutrinos through each square centimetre of you, every second

cards.title: Neutrinos are pouring through you right now

cards.body: US stocks slid on November 5 as investors dumped AI and semiconductor shares. The Nasdaq fell into a correction, meaning 10% below its recent high. Here are the one-day drops.
cards.more:
The Dow lost about 1,833 points. Nvidia, Micron and AMD were among the big decliners.
Wall Street's fear gauge, the VIX, jumped by about 70%.
cards.title: Chip stocks fell hardest in Thursday's sell-off

beats: Bacteriophages, or phages, are viruses that infect only bacteria, never human cells.
A phage lands on a bacterium, latches onto a specific surface molecule, and injects its DNA.
That DNA hijacks the cell's machinery to build dozens of new phages inside it.
The phages then burst the cell open and go hunting for the next bacterium.
Each phage targets a narrow range of strains, so doctors must match the phage to the infection.
cards.more:
Phages were discovered over a century ago, around 1915 to 1917, but antibiotics overshadowed them in the West.
Rising antibiotic resistance has revived interest, especially for infections nothing else can treat.
cards.title: How a virus can kill bacteria for us

beats: A correction is a fall of at least 10% from a recent peak.
A bear market is a deeper fall, usually 20% or more from the peak.
The thresholds are conventions, not laws; nothing special happens at exactly 10%.
Corrections are fairly common and many recover within months, though some deepen.
The labels describe the past move; they do not predict what comes next.
cards.title: What 'correction' and 'bear market' actually mean

beats: Normally, trade winds push warm surface water west across the tropical Pacific toward Asia.
In an El Niño, those winds weaken and the warm water sloshes back east toward South America.
Warm water feeds rising air and storms, so rainfall patterns shift with it.
Those shifts ripple through the atmosphere, bringing droughts to some regions and floods to others.
Because the ocean also releases heat, El Niño years tend to push global temperatures up.
cards.title: How El Niño reshuffles the world's weather

beats: Suppose someone claims to have a complete list of all prime numbers.
Multiply every prime on the list together, then add one.
Dividing that number by any listed prime always leaves a remainder of one.
So its prime factors must be missing from the list.
No list can be complete; Euclid proved this about 2,300 years ago.
cards.title: Why the primes never run out

beats: Lab experiments are slow and costly, so you cannot test every candidate molecule.
A model learns patterns from known examples, such as what real hormones look like.
It scores thousands of untested candidates by how closely they fit those patterns.
Scientists then test only the top few in the lab.
The AI suggests; the experiments decide whether the suggestion was right.
cards.title: How AI narrows a haystack before scientists search it

beats: Spoken words are built from small sound units called phonemes, like the c-a-t in 'cat'.
Children first learn to hear and juggle these sounds, often through rhymes and word games.
Reading means linking letters to those sounds and blending them into words.
A child who can't hear the separate sounds has nothing for the letters to attach to.
Vocabulary then turns the decoded word into meaning, which is why both skills matter.
cards.title: Why hearing sounds inside words unlocks reading

beats: A SQUID is a loop of superconducting wire broken by one or two ultra-thin barriers.
In a superconducting loop, magnetic flux comes only in fixed, tiny steps.
The current through the barriers swings sharply as the field changes by a fraction of a step.
That makes SQUIDs among the most sensitive magnetic field detectors ever built.
Hospitals use them to map the faint magnetic fields of brain activity, called MEG.
cards.title: What a SQUID is, and why it can sense your brainwaves

myth.claim: Eating sugar makes children hyper and hard to control.
myth.truth: Double-blind trials, where nobody knew who got sugar, found no effect on behaviour. Parents who merely believed their child had sugar rated them as more hyperactive. Exciting settings like parties likely explain the rest.

cards.title: Sugar makes kids hyperactive

myth.claim: Astronauts float because there's no gravity in orbit.
myth.truth: At the station's height, gravity is still about 90% as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they and the station are falling together around Earth, moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it.

cards.title: There's no gravity on the space station

myth.claim: Napoleon Bonaparte was famously short.
myth.truth: He was about 1.69 m (5 ft 7 in), average or a bit above for a Frenchman of his time. Confusion between French and English inches, British cartoons, and his nickname 'the little corporal' built the legend.

cards.title: Napoleon was tiny

quiz.q: Which gas makes up the largest share of Earth's atmosphere?
quiz.why: Nitrogen is about 78% of dry air; oxygen is about 21%, argon nearly 1%, and CO2 only about 0.04%.

cards.title: What is most of the air you breathe?

quiz.q: 0.999... with nines repeating forever is:
quiz.why: One third is 0.333..., and three thirds is 0.999..., which is 1. No number fits between them, so they are the same.

cards.title: Is 0.999... really equal to 1?

quiz.q: 'Clue' grew out of an old word for what?
quiz.why: A 'clew' was a ball of yarn. In the Greek myth, Theseus unwound one to find his way out of the labyrinth, so a clue became anything that guides you to an answer.

cards.title: Where does the word 'clue' come from?

cards.body: Hubble has no engine, and air drag is slowly lowering its orbit; NASA expects reentry around 2033 to 2034. On October 29 the agency asked industry for ideas: boost it higher, service it, or retire it safely. A boost would need to happen by 2032.
cards.more:
The request for information is open until November 30. It is a survey of what technology exists, not an approved mission.
The three options on the table are a spacecraft that pushes Hubble to a higher orbit, a servicing mission to upgrade it, or a controlled descent into the atmosphere or disposal in orbit.
Hubble is run from NASA Goddard, with science operations at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore and ESA as a partner.
cards.title: NASA is asking companies how to rescue Hubble before it falls

cards.body: ESA's Hera spacecraft photographed Didymos and its small moon Dimorphos as two separate objects on October 18, from about 1,280 km away. NASA's DART probe slammed into Dimorphos in 2022. Hera will now study the crash site, with its first detailed images due on November 25.
cards.more:
Dimorphos is about 151 metres across and circles Didymos, which is about 780 metres wide, at a distance of roughly 1.15 km.
DART's 2022 impact shortened that orbit by about 33 minutes, more than simulations predicted. Nobody yet knows whether it left a crater or reshaped the whole asteroid.
Hera slowed to 20 metres per second relative to the pair after two thruster burns in early October. It will release two shoebox-sized CubeSats to help measure mass and internal structure.
cards.title: Hera has the asteroid pair that DART hit in its sights

cards.body: Radio images from 2021 to 2026 show Betelgeuse looking more stretched when a suspected companion star, Siwarha, is farthest to one side, and rounder when it passes in front or behind. Astronomers call it strong evidence the companion disturbs the giant's outer layers, though more observations are needed.
cards.more:
Siwarha was first proposed in 2024 to explain a roughly 2,100-day brightness cycle. It is too faint to see directly at radio wavelengths.
The team, led by Lynn Matthews of MIT Haystack Observatory, used the VLA and ALMA telescopes at seven frequencies. They also mapped a cool layer in the star's atmosphere at about 2,200 kelvin.
The work appears in The Astronomical Journal.
cards.title: A hidden companion may be stirring Betelgeuse's atmosphere

cards.body: A SLAC-led team fired circularly polarised X-rays at manganese telluride, long filed as an ordinary antiferromagnet. They measured a 'handed' signal that only an altermagnet should produce. Altermagnets have no overall magnetic pull, yet can steer electron spins, which could help future memory chips.
cards.more:
For decades, magnets came in two families: ferromagnets and antiferromagnets. The name altermagnet was only coined in 2022.
The team ran the experiment at the European Synchrotron in France in 2024 and reproduced it in early 2025. The paper is in Science.
Useful devices are still a long way off. The next step is learning to control these magnetic states with light and electricity.
cards.title: X-rays caught a third kind of magnetism in action

cards.body: Quark-gluon plasma, the matter that filled the universe in its first millionths of a second, was thought to need heavy nuclei like lead. All four big LHC experiments now report signs of it in collisions of much lighter oxygen and neon nuclei. Several results are still preliminary.
cards.more:
The plasma forms at more than 100,000 times the temperature at the Sun's core. Quarks and gluons, normally locked inside protons and neutrons, flow freely.
The main clue is that fast particles lose energy crossing the fireball, so fewer emerge than in proton collisions. Physicists note that a drop in particles alone doesn't prove energy loss.
The findings come a year after the LHC's first-ever oxygen collisions.
cards.title: Even small atoms can make the Big Bang's hot soup

cards.body: In a 2025 Anthropic experiment, researchers injected a concept's activity pattern into a language model; the most capable version flagged the intrusion in about 20% of trials.
